title: Case Study: Schuit Sustainable Development Project on Stavos

paragraphs.text: SSDP is a project development company based in the Netherlands, with branches in a number of European countries.

The Mediterranean island of Stavos has approximately 6,800 permanent inhabitants. Tourism is increasing annually with a total of 776,000 overnight stays last year, 90% of which took place during the summer. In parallel, there is considerable activity from mineral extraction. The economy of the island relies on these two industries.

Drinking water has always been in very short supply on Stavos, as the island has no significant drinking water resources of its own. Up to now, the island has relied on rainwater, mainland water delivered by ships, and drillings. Only the first two options provided drinkable water. The drillings provided water of high salt and mineral content, which led to corrosion when used in machines and household appliances.

The main objective of the Stavos project was the provision of drinking water. In addition, SSDP aimed to ensure the successful renovation of the grid which carries water to users throughout the island. This would in turn support the project’s third objective, which was to create a sustainable installation to make heating available to the larger agglomerations on Stavos during the winter months.

In order to achieve its main objective SSDP chose, as the most sustainable solution, to desalinate seawater using geothermal energy from below the earth. The energy needed for desalination is provided by geothermal fluids pumped from the crust, where temperatures reach 100°C. The pure water produced by this process then requires cooling, and thermal energy from the same source can also be used at this stage. In addition, the system used on Stavos produces sufficient electricity for both the pumping of the geothermal fluid and its re-injection back into the earth’s crust, meaning that operating costs are low.

The geological and physical preconditions for the project are ideal, but community acceptance of geothermal projects on the island was at its lowest possible point when SSDP presented the project idea. This was due to an unsuccessful attempt by the National Power Corporation in the 1980s to produce electricity using high enthalpy* geothermal energy. Due to bad maintenance, the blow-out of a faulty drilling head in a spot above the main village of the island led to the outflow of high pressure geothermal steam at over 300°C. This caused earth movements and noise, and deposited chemicals on the main village.

This event, and the lack of information provided to the local community about the risks involved, had a negative impact on community attitudes towards any future geothermal projects on the island. To overcome this, SSDP initially made it clear that every step of the project would be discussed with the community. SSDP opened an office on the island and employed a local resident to provide information to the public. At the beginning of the project, all Stavos citizens were invited to a meeting and provided with the opportunity to express their fears concerning the proposed project; they also discussed all potential obstacles. Special information releases were distributed at key points on the island, such as the Town Hall and other authorities, hotels, restaurants, travel agencies, etc.

In addition, the company constructed two water tanks with 500 m³ capacity each, for the storage of drinking water brought to the island by ships, as an interim solution until local water production commenced. A former area of wasteland on the island was also replanted with indigenous plants and opened as a botanical garden.

The first stage of the project has now been successfully implemented. As a result, the total cost of drinkable water on Stavos has been significantly reduced. While consumers previously paid an average of 395 €/m³ for bottled water, SSDP is now producing water for under 2 €/m³. Local agriculture is profiting from the introduction of irrigation schemes, and groundwater levels are showing signs of recovery. Additional savings factors are also being realised, for example in the form of the increased life expectancy of household appliances (e.g. washing machines) and industrial equipment which, when run with clean water, require less maintenance, resulting in lower costs. The use of water bottles has been reduced, meaning that there is less waste to be disposed of and less litter. The improved water supply means that tourism may increase further, creating additional jobs (although precautions must be taken to avoid possible risks for the environment with the increase in tourism).
After completion of the two stages of the project, SSDP plans to duplicate this concept in at least four other islands in the region.
